short: The first Chinese dynasty attested by its own written records, on oracle bones.
full:
The Shang ruled the middle and lower Yellow River from about 1600 BCE, moving their capital several times before settling at Yin, near modern Anyang. Excavation there from 1928 recovered tens of thousands of inscribed ox scapulae and turtle plastrons: questions put to ancestors and the high god Di about harvests, childbirth, hunting and war, with the answers read from heat cracks. Those texts carry the earliest known Chinese writing and confirm a king list close to the one Sima Qian recorded a millennium later.

Shang power rested on bronze and horses. Its foundries produced ritual vessels of a technical quality unmatched anywhere at the time, cast in ceramic piece moulds rather than by lost wax, and its armies fought from spoke-wheeled chariots. Royal tombs at Anyang contain chariots, weapons and the remains of sacrificed retainers and prisoners. In about 1046 BCE the last king, Di Xin, was defeated by the Zhou at Muye and the dynasty ended. The dates remain approximate, resting on radiocarbon and astronomical reconstruction rather than dated documents.
